title: The Paramāras and the Foundation of Udaypur: Kingship, Patronage and Urban Formation

sections.title: From feudatories to kings of Malwa
sections.plan_title: From feudatories to kings of Malwa
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows four things: - the Paramāras first appear as Rāṣṭrakūṭa feudatories in Gujarat; - Sīyaka's claim to a sovereign title brought war, and the Paramāras sacked Mānyakheṭa in 972–73; - the first royal charter issued from Malwa itself dates from 975; - the dynasty's own genealogy, kept at Udaypur, magnifies these kings in ways their editors do not accept.
sections.transition: Within a generation of Sīyaka, the eastern limit was held by a king whose reputation would outrun his kingdom.

paras.first: The next claim made about this country comes from the west.
paras.last: Limits of this kind mark the edge of a state, not the holder of any one hill inside it, and the earliest charters of the house that drew them were issued far from Udaypur, in Gujarat.
paras.plan_point: Take up 3.5. The district Gazetteer credits Sīyaka II with ousting the Chandellas from Malwa and with a kingdom bounded on the east by Vidisha. Other modern accounts give the same eastern limit at his abdication. This is a frontier, not a holder of Udaypur's hill.

paras.first: The oldest are two grants issued on the bank of the Mahi by Sīyaka, who is styled in them both *Mahārājādhirāja*, king of kings, and “the crest-jewel among the feudatories”.
paras.last: Their verses give the line as Bappaiparāja, Vairisiṃha and Sīyaka, each the son and successor of the one before, and by allowing twenty-five years to each ruler the editor of the Paramāra inscriptions puts the start of Bappaiparāja's career about 900.
paras.plan_title: Feudatories who took a king's title
paras.plan_point: The earliest grants place the family in Gujarat. At Harsola in 949, Sīyaka is both *Mahārājādhirāja* and "crest-jewel among the feudatories", and the grants name his line back to Bappaiparāja (c. 900).

paras.first: The higher title had consequences.
paras.last: A grant of October 969 shows Sīyaka still on the throne, and the one his son Vākpati-Muñja made in 975 is the first royal charter of the house issued from Malwa rather than from Gujarat.
paras.plan_point: The title probably provoked the Rāṣṭrakūṭa expedition. The Paramāras answered at Khalighaṭṭa on the Narmadā and then sacked Mānyakheṭa in 972–73, a date fixed by Dhanapāla's colophon. Sīyaka was still ruling in 969. Vākpati-Muñja's grant of 975 is the first royal charter of the house issued from Malwa.

paras.first: Vākpati-Muñja's end shows how far the dynasty's later account could run ahead of its fortunes.
paras.last: He is known chiefly from Padmagupta's *Navasāhasānka-carita*, which also credits him with successes against Kosala, Vāgaḍa and the Muralas.
paras.plan_title: What Udaypur's stone claims for them
paras.plan_point: Muñja died a captive of the Chālukya Tailapa II between 993–94 and 997–98. Yet the Udaypur praśasti has the Karṇāṭas, Lāṭas, Keralas and Cholas at his feet and his sword raised in Tripurī. The editor finds no evidence for Tripurī and calls the Karṇāṭa claim "evidently inadmissible". Sindhurāja has half a verse and is known mainly from a poet. *(Evidence pass: C04-CII-129 is the Udaypur praśasti's own claim; it sets up "claim, not event" on Udaypur's stone.)*

paras.first: The same stone is the only record that gives the early line complete, and its portraits of those first kings are, in the editor's judgement, purely conventional.
paras.last: What the dynasty said of itself, and what its grants and its enemies' inscriptions allow, part company from the start, and the fullest statement of that self-image is the one cut at Udaypur.
paras.plan_point: Brief. The praśasti alone gives the early line complete (recall 1.4 in a clause), and its descriptions of those kings are "purely conventional". Its first ruler, Upendra, is the Kṛṣṇarāja of the grants.

sections.title: Bhoja's kingdom and Bhoja's name
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows three things: - Bhoja's dated reign (1011–1047) and the date by which the Bhopal country is known to have been his (1018); - the model of royal building and learning his name carried: Bhojpur, the Vāgdevī image, a Śaiva treatise; - that at Udaypur his fame survives first as praise cut by his successors, which modern writers have extended into memory.
sections.transition: The praśasti that praises Bhoja passes over the king who came next.

paras.first: Bhoja's dated records run from the Mōdāsā grant of V.S. 1067 (1011) to the Tilakawāḍā grant of V.S. 1103 (1047).
paras.last: None of the records that fix the frontier in his reign was found at Udaypur itself.
paras.plan_point: Bhoja's dated records run from the Mōdāsā grant (1011) to the Tilakawāḍā grant (1047). The first Paramāra charter in the Bhopal territory (1018) shows that country already in his kingdom. In 1030 Al-Bīrūnī put the kingdom's eastern limit at Bhilsa. Udaypur's country lay inside that edge, but no record of Bhoja's time names it.

paras.first: The reputation that later gathered round the house was largely Bhoja's, and it rested on works as much as on wars.
paras.last: Bhoja is credited with a work of the Śaiva Siddhānta, the *Tattvaprakāśa*, on the three principles of the Lord, the individual soul and its fetters, and a popular account adds a large treatise on architecture, the *Samarangana-sutradhara*.
paras.plan_title: A king who built and wrote
paras.plan_point: The model his name carried: - the Bhojpur temple, begun but never finished, linked to a colossal dam (2.4 told the dam; one clause); - the Vāgdevī image of 1033–34, engraved by Manathala; - a Śaiva Siddhānta treatise, the *Tattvaprakāśa*, ascribed to him. Doubts about his authorship go in a note.

paras.first: Udaypur's own stone praises him in those terms, though it was cut after his death.
paras.last: It describes what an ideal Paramāra king should be, in his successors' words, and very few remains of so extensive a programme can now be traced.
paras.plan_point: At Udaypur, Bhoja's fame survives as praise cut by his successors. The praśasti gives him verses 16–20: his strength, gifts, victories and temples, and a realm "from Kailāsa to Malaya". Verse 20 says he "covered the world all around with temples" to Kedāra, Rāmeśvara, Somanātha and others, which the editor reads as the four quarters. Few remains of such work can now be traced. That this is praise, not an inventory, was said in 1.4 (recall).

paras.first: The next verse turns from praise to loss.
paras.last: It names no enemy, but they were powerful enough to have deprived the Paramāras of their kingdom in Bhoja's last days or just after his death.

paras.first: Modern writing about Udaypur draws Bhoja closer still.
paras.last: The stone that praises him at such length passes over the king who reigned next.
paras.plan_point: Modern Udaypur writing draws Bhoja closer than the record does. Tiwari sees a "deep relation" between the town and Bhoja, and imagines Udayāditya preparing for kingship under his protection. Popular books make Bhoja a founder of cities. The record gives no act of Bhoja at Udaypur; it gives only the praśasti's statement that Udayāditya followed him on the throne. Memory, told as memory.

unmatched_plan.title: Bhoja's end, in a clause
unmatched_plan.point: Bhoja died some time before 1055 (1.2 told how).

sections.title: The broken succession and the recovery
sections.plan_title: The broken succession and the recovery
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows four things: - the dynasty's own praśastis leave Bhoja's successor Jayasiṃha out, though his grants place him between 1047 and 1080; - a record of V.S. 1116 from Vāgaḍa suggests (the editor's presumption) a struggle in which Udayāditya may have been Jayasiṃha's adversary; - the coalition that overwhelmed Jayasiṃha was three-sided and is reconstructed differently by the editor, in two lists, and by Ganguly; - Udayāditya's victory is praised on Udaypur's second slab, and his relation to Bhoja stays disputed, for reasons that matter to Udaypur.
sections.transition: That eastern territory comes with a date, V.S. 1116, eleven years before the accession.

paras.first: The king who reigned next was Jayasiṃha, who regained his hereditary kingdom with the help of the Cālukya king Someśvara.
paras.last: The dynasty's own list of its kings has a gap where a reigning king should stand, and the gap falls just before the man whose name Udaypur bears.
paras.plan_point: Recall in one clause Jayasiṃha's restoration (1.2). New: the Udaypur and Nagpur praśastis, which list almost every king, omit him. His own grant names him Bhoja's immediate successor, and the editor places him "between 1047 and 1080". The panegyric's silence is a choice.

paras.first: The year later read as Udaypur's beginning finds Jayasiṃha acknowledged as king.
paras.last: The record itself names no rival, and its other possibility is as open as the first.
paras.plan_point: The Pānāheḍā inscription of V.S. 1116 (1059) shows Maṇḍalika of Vāgaḍa "greatly devoted" to Jayasiṃha. The editor presumes that Maṇḍalika's son may have helped Jayasiṃha against "his adversary Udayāditya or some other person". A possibility only, but it bears on 4.4: the year read as Udaypur's beginning is a year of Jayasiṃha's acknowledged rule.

paras.first: What finally overwhelmed Jayasiṃha was a coalition.
paras.last: He is also credited with subduing rebellious feudatories, and with a stability in which the art and literature of Malwa flourished.
paras.plan_point: New against 1.2: the shape of the second invasion. Udayāditya's son's record counts three enemies. In the editor's fuller account these were: - the Kalachuri Karṇa; - the Chālukya Someśvara II, whose general, the Gaṅga Udayāditya, came with the Hoysala Ereyaṅga. Someśvara II was quarrelling with his brother Vikramāditya, Jayasiṃha's ally. Jayasiṃha was "possibly" killed. Ganguly tells it otherwise: the Caulukyas and Karṇāṭas held Dhārā, and Udayāditya won with cavalry from the Cāhamāna Durlabha III against the "Gurjara" Karṇa. The text keeps the event; the identities go to a note.

paras.first: Udaypur's own slabs carry the dynasty's version of the victory.
paras.last: In 1076 Vikramāditya VI overthrew his brother Someśvara II, and the former ally of the house turned against Udayāditya; an inscription of 1077 from Shikarpur taluq calls Vikramāditya “a great fever of terror to the king of Dhārā”.
paras.plan_title: Udaypur's second slab, and a war that went on
paras.plan_point: 1.4 told the second slab's rout of the lord of Chedi (recall in a clause). New: - the editor uses it to answer Bühler's doubt about Bhoja's reverse; - the slab's last complete verse says that for him who had restored the earth "it was easy to restore the Primeval Boar", which the editor takes as a hint that Udayāditya restored a Boar temple, recorded in the lost portion. This is the editor's inference only. - Peace did not last: after Vikramāditya VI took the Chālukya throne in 1076, an inscription of 1077 calls him "a great fever of terror to the king of Dhārā" (Ganguly).

paras.first: Who Udayāditya was matters here as much as what he did.
paras.last: The Udayapura pedigree also states that Udayāditya was ruling in V.S. 1116, years before his accession.
paras.plan_title: Why his descent matters at Udaypur
paras.plan_point: One sentence with the canon wording: a kinsman of Bhoja; the exact relationship is disputed (1.2's note holds the readings; do not repeat them). New: - The question is Udaypur's because the "junior branch" view would give Udayāditya ground of his own in the east before he was king. That view rests on a pedigree from an Udaypur inscription in which Udayāditya, "having obtained the eastern territory", proceeded into Malwa, which his ancestors had once governed. - Verma, as Tiwari reports, holds that "meditating at the feet" (*pādānudhyāta*) is a formula of praise, used even of Chandragupta II's commanders, and proves no descent. - Tiwari asks why no record of Bhoja's time names a brother.

sections.title: Before the throne? The dates and what rests on them
sections.plan_title: Before the throne? The dates and what rests on them
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows four things: - that "begun in 1059" is Ganguly's reading of late records: a fragmentary record he himself dates 1513 and calls full of "gross mistakes", and a pedigree record that CII dates to V.S. 1562 and rejects; - that modern handbooks and surveys repeat the year without adding a witness; - that 1080 stands on a record on the temple itself; - that his reign is followed year by year from 1080, with c. 1070 the working accession.
sections.transition: If the record makes him king first and patron at Udaypur second, the question becomes what Udaypur was to that king.

paras.first: A beginning in 1059 has many supporters.
paras.last: He resolved the difficulty by assuming that Udayāditya built the temple in 1059 “when he was ruling his paternal territory apparently from Udayapur”.
paras.plan_title: The case for 1059, at its strongest
paras.plan_point: Give it fairly: - the district Gazetteer: two temple inscriptions refer to work begun in V.S. 1116, and it calls the building's years "abundantly clear"; - Patil gives the same span; - Hardy writes "founded … in 1059 and consecrated in 1080"; - Kramrisch's caption gives c. 1059–1087; - the survey gives one foundation year for the town, the temple and the lake. Behind them stands Ganguly, who found Udayāditya "ruling in Sam 1116" and reconciled this with the accession by a reign in his paternal territory, "apparently from Udayapur". (1.2 noted the reconciliation; here it is the point.)

paras.first: Followed back to their sources, these statements rest on three witnesses, none of them an edited contemporary record.
paras.last: It is less secure than 1080 because each of its witnesses is late, faulty or both.
paras.plan_point: U6. Trace each support: - **(a)** The statement that Udayāditya built the temple in V.S. 1116 comes from the fragmentary record Ganguly dates 1513 and himself calls "very perfunctorily executed" and full of "gross mistakes" (1.5, recall in a clause). - **(b)** The statement that he was ruling in V.S. 1116 comes from the Udaypur pedigree (4.3 P5). The CII editor dates that record V.S. 1562 (1505/06) and rejects its genealogy against the Dōngargāon and Jainad records. - **(c)** The two late records are not identified with each other in any item; keep them apart (Part I, C1-B). The handbooks and surveys add no independent witness. The inscription on the temple that the surveys read as V.S. 1116 has no edition in the corpus (note).

paras.first: The year 1080 stands on firmer ground.
paras.last: The firm date, for its part, marks a stage in the temple's life rather than its beginning, since the record of 1080 has been read as a consecration, as the raising of a flag-staff and as its repair.
paras.plan_title: The other side of the scale
paras.plan_point: - The CII editor: the Udaypur record of V.S. 1137 (1080) "supplies the earliest known date for the king Udayāditya", and names the temple Udayeśvaradeva, "evidently after the name of its constructor". - The flag-hoisting record is in situ on the temple. - The Pānāheḍā record of V.S. 1116 shows Jayasiṃha acknowledged that very year (4.3 P2), and Ganguly's own argument from Karṇa shows Udayāditya could not then have been sovereign. - A lord building on his own ground before his accession is possible, on a late record. It is not shown. - Recall 1.4's three readings of the 1080 record in a clause.

paras.first: Much rests on the choice.
paras.last: The evidence allows the second firmly and the first only on late or faulty testimony, and the question of a town begun before its founder was king stays open.

paras.first: Set that year aside, and the reign's own records carry it forward.
paras.last: The earlier starting years given for the reign depend on the reading just traced.
paras.plan_point: - **The dated records:** - 1080, Udaypur; - 1081, an image consecrated at Dhārā by Jasahara; - a gift by Naravarman, made while Udayāditya was encamped at Dhavalī near Ujjain, for a perpetual lamp for his dead brother Lakṣmadeva; - 1086–87, a Śambhu temple at Jhālrapāṭan built by the *paṭṭakila* Jannaka of an oilman's lineage "when Udayāditya was prosperous in the region"; - a royal endowment to Somanātha on the fort of Kōśavardhana. - **The span:** the reign runs to his death in 1093 (4.5). - **The accession:** c. 1070 is the working position. The earlier starts (1058, 1059) rest on the same 1059 reading (interpretive, said once; the list of datings was in 1.2's note: recall, do not list).

sections.title: A town with a king's name
sections.plan_title: A town with a king's name
sections.statement: By the end, the reader knows five things: - what the name proves (a king's name on a temple, and on a town and tank by a later report) and what it does not (a founding); - that one damaged record makes Udayapura the seat of a subordinate Nēmaka house under the king; - that the provincial geography often attached to his Udaypur belongs to the 1170s; - how later writers have pictured his town; - that the reign ended in 1093, with Naravarman succeeding and a memorial gift in 1095. The one work a contemporary record ties to him at Udaypur is the temple that bears his name.

paras.first: At Udaypur the king's name is the one link to him that the records make certain.
paras.last: A name, though, can be given to a new town or laid upon an older one, and none of the inscriptions of the reign says which happened at Udaypur.
paras.plan_point: Recall the triad (1.2) in a clause. New: - the 1080 record names the temple after its constructor; - Patil and Ganguly report another inscription in the temple that credits him with town, temple and tank; - Ganguly also cites "a contemporary inscription" that the city was built by Udayāditya, though the item does not name it; - later writers turn the name into a founding outright: he "laid the foundation of the city" (Ganguly), "founded the city" (Pande); INTACH and Adhikari follow. A royal temple was a royal gift (*dāna*), bringing merit to the giver: a king who named a temple after himself gave in his own name. Name ≠ foundation: 1.5's question is sharpened, not closed.

paras.first: The village has its own answer, and the survey has placed it on the ground.
paras.last: The legend is memory of a conquest, and its location on the ground a proposal; together they keep open the possibility that Udayāditya's name was laid upon a place already lived in.

paras.first: One damaged record gives the place a role in his reign's government.
paras.last: It rests on a single abraded slab.
paras.plan_title: A seat for a subordinate house
paras.plan_point: 1.2 gave the reading in one sentence; here it is the subject: - the damaged slab calls Udayapura the capital town of the Nēmaka dynasty, "which was subordinate to Udayāditya"; - its object appears to be that the place was put in charge of a Nēmaka king, by whom, or in whose reign, a temple was built; - his father Śūdraka is said to have defeated a king of Gujarat, possibly the Caulukya Karṇa, which sets the house in Udayāditya's time. Which temple is meant is not stated. Tiwari, reporting readers of the script, gives the Nēmakas as Śiva worshippers and surmises that they administered the place when the temple was begun. That surmise goes in a note.

paras.first: The record that has done most to describe the town's surrounding country belongs to a later century.
paras.last: The district, the sub-district and its officer describe Udayapura's rank in the generations after him, not the circumstances of its founding.
paras.plan_title: A province described eighty years later
paras.plan_point: - the district Gazetteer attributes to Udayāditya a record of 1173 that describes Udayapur's province (the Bhilsa *maṇḍala*, the Bhṛṅgārikā *pāṭhaka* of sixty-four villages, a *daṇḍanāyaka* probably seated at Udayapur); - Udayāditya died in 1093, and in the 1170s the province was governed for the Caulukyas (1.3, as corrected); - the Mahādvādaśaka-maṇḍala is a twelfth-century name. The province is evidence for the town's later rank, not for his founding.

paras.first: Modern writing pictures the town he left more fully than any record does.
paras.last: No record of the reign dates the walls, the palace or the tanks, and the evidence for their building lies in the fabric itself.
paras.plan_title: The town as it has been pictured
paras.plan_point: In Tiwari's telling, the town was planned: - square, walled, with the king's palace inside; - a "mini-capital" on the Kalachuri frontier, made important by its sandstone; - with a great hall and Sanskrit school "on the lines of" Bhoja's foundations. Ganguly lists Udayapura among the towns that rose to importance under the dynasty. The walls, the palace and the tanks are dated by no record of this reign (Ch 7 treats their fabric). The land is setting, not cause (no "because of the quarries").

paras.first: What the records do follow is the king's own end.
paras.last: Of all the works later writers give him at Udaypur, from the town's foundation to its walls and lakes, one is tied to his reign by a record of the time: the temple that bears his name, whose flag-hoisting a stone on the temple records in V.S. 1137.
paras.plan_title: The king's death, and what Udaypur keeps
paras.plan_point: - Lakṣmadeva died before his father; Naravarman's lamp gift shows it. - A further son, Jagaddeva, is praised for refusing the throne out of regard for an elder brother. - Udayāditya died in the latter part of 1093. Naravarman succeeded in V.S. 1151 (1094), and in V.S. 1152 (1095) made a gift at his father's annual funeral rite. - Close: of all that later writers give him at Udaypur, a contemporary record ties one work to his reign, the temple that bears his name. This hands the chapter to Ch 5.

opening: The next claim made about this country comes from the west.
closing: Of all the works later writers give him at Udaypur, from the town's foundation to its walls and lakes, one is tied to his reign by a record of the time: the temple that bears his name, whose flag-hoisting a stone on the temple records in V.S. 1137.
opening_para: The next claim made about this country comes from the west.
